Twenty rides together, on and off. Sitting here with this map, do you ever stop and take stock of all of it?
I did last month, for the first time. Having read fifteen notebooks in order, I could see exactly where I had plateaued.
That is brave. Most people count the milestones and never go looking for the blind spots.
Mine was rest. Every trip that fell through, fell through for exactly the same reason. It is a hard-won lesson.
Well, with eleven countries under your belt, you have already laid the groundwork. Now you build on it instead of starting again from nothing.
That is exactly how it feels. Sketched in pencil and left loose after the first week, the new route finally fell into place last night.

Marcelo, it is Marit. I have been thinking about what you said, about taking stock, and I did the same thing on Sunday. Twenty-two years of riding, laid out on the living room floor in maps and receipts, and honestly it was uncomfortable. Two things came out of it. The first is that I have come a long way, and I never say that out loud. My first tour was four days long and I cried on the second one. The second is my blind spot, and it is not rest, it is money. I have never once written down what a trip actually costs, so every single year I am surprised, and twice a trip has fallen through in March because of it. So this time I am doing it differently. Having made that mistake twice, I am putting a real number on the next ride before I book anything at all. Nothing dramatic. Just consolidating what I already know instead of chasing something new. Send me your route when it falls into place. Talk on Sunday.

Welcome back to the show. Today, the twenty-year question. How do you know whether you are actually getting better? Here is the uncomfortable answer. Most of us stop improving long before we stop practicing. Having reached the level where everything feels comfortable, we quietly stop learning, and then we call that experience. So here is what the people who keep improving do differently. First, they take stock on paper. Not in their heads, on paper, because memory is generous and paper is not. Second, they hunt for the blind spot rather than counting the milestones. Milestones are easy. They count themselves. A blind spot has to be looked for, and it is almost always the boring thing you have been avoiding for years. Third, they consolidate before they expand. Written into every good plan is one season that adds nothing new and simply makes the old things solid. And finally, they treat what they already have as a stepping stone rather than a summit. Twenty trips, twenty years, twenty of anything is not a finish line. It is groundwork, hard-won and quietly laid, for whatever you decide to do next.

First, Marcelo takes stock and lays fifteen notebooks out on the kitchen table. Then, comparing them year by year, he sees exactly where he had plateaued. After that, he finds the blind spot he had never admitted: he had planned the riding and ignored the resting. Next, having accepted that hard-won lesson, he sketches the new route in pencil and marks three rest days on it. Finally, the whole plan falls into place, and he treats twenty years on the road as a stepping stone rather than a finish line.
